title: What would you test after an AI-assisted turn-sync change passes on localhost?
author: biggdogg420
selftext:
I’m working on LAN multiplayer for BOTF Remastered, a turn-based strategy fan project. Claude co-authored the change that has each peer compute a fingerprint of its game state after resolving a turn. If those fingerprints disagree, the game flags the turn and can resync from the host’s state.

The commit records a local development test. Two instances on one PC agreed on their fingerprints for 13 turns over localhost. In a separate run, we deliberately made one instance diverge. The game caught the mismatch on that turn, the host sent its state, and the peers agreed again on subsequent turns. The clean run showed the peers could stay in sync on one machine. Forcing the failure showed the check could actually detect a disagreement and that we had a way to recover.

[Commit and author-reported test notes](https://github.com/thabiggdogg420-a11y/botf-remake/commit/b8e18efd82d3e988e9f05d08d4c5f9e40adbb3d5)

LAN is still unreleased. These were local desktop instances. The public 0.1.468 browser beta is a separate build, and this test gives us no end-to-end web multiplayer result.

If you’ve shipped turn-based multiplayer, which failure would you require us to test across two machines before a LAN beta? I’d start by dropping and reconnecting a client with orders pending, then checking whether those orders execute once after the client rejoins. What case would you put ahead of that?
